The most an off-tick reading can differ from the model

Source: R/nomogram.R
mm_reading_error.Rd

A bound, not a probe. The quantity is attained by some profile a clinician could read, so it answers "how wrong can this nomogram be between its printed ticks" rather than "how wrong was it at the places I happened to look".

Usage

mm_reading_error(nom, model, per_gap = 5L)

Arguments

nom

An rms nomogram.

model

A mm_model().

per_gap

Interior points scanned in each gap between ticks. Cost is linear in it and in the number of axes, and the answer is stable well below the default.

Value

A list: bound, the largest absolute risk difference any reading between ticks can carry; lp, the same bound on the linear-predictor scale; and by_axis, each axis's own error range, which is where to look when the bound is too large and the question is which axis needs more ticks. bound and lp are NA when no axis has two ticks to read between, because then there is no off-tick reading to make.

Why a bound is computable without searching the joint space

Total points are additive across axes and the printed linear-predictor axis is affine in them, so for any profile

$$lp_{nomogram} - lp_{model} = b \sum_j e_j(x_j)$$

where \(e_j\) is one axis's linear-interpolation error in points and \(b\) is the points-to-lp slope. Each \(e_j\) is zero at that axis's own ticks, which is what the tick-agreement check in mm_nomogram() establishes, and each is free to take its own worst value because the predictors are chosen independently. So the extremes of the sum are the sums of the extremes, and one scan per axis is enough: no search over combinations of predictors is needed, and none is done.

Each axis is scanned with every other predictor sitting on a tick, so the discrepancy observed is exactly that axis's. An axis is scanned once per stratum it is drawn in, because an interaction with a factor gives a continuous predictor a different points curve per level and rms draws those as separate axes: on one fixture the age error ran to -0.046 in one stratum where the other reached only -0.006, so a single stratum is not a bound over both.

The worst total error in points becomes a worst error in risk through the logistic, whose steepest point is the one that matters: \(\max_u |plogis(u + \delta) - plogis(u)|\) is attained at \(u = -\delta/2\), that is at a risk of one half. The bound does not ask whether a profile with that risk also attains the worst points error, so it holds whether or not one does.

What it does not cover

Interpolation only. Not the clinician's eye on the printed page, not a total falling off the drawn scale, which mm_nomogram() counts separately as off_axis, and not a predictor outside the range the model was developed on, which mm_predict() marks as .extrapolated. It is also a numerical bound rather than an analytic one: each axis is scanned on a finite grid, so a sharper extremum could sit between two scanned points. Measured, that slack is about one part in a thousand: raising per_gap from 3 to 25 moved the lp bound from 0.12613 to 0.12626 on a two-spline fixture whose worst observed reading was 0.0215 against a bound of 0.0315. The slack runs an order of magnitude smaller than the margin the bound already carries.
